watch.summary.back: This animated video discusses how to choose news. Not long ago, most people got news from only a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources can even disagree about facts. The video gives some tips. If you can, look for the first source, like the original report or speech. If a big news story is still developing, don't check it every few minutes. Wait until the facts are clear. Read the same news in more than one place. Watch for words like "allegedly", "most likely", or "maybe". Those words show that the report is not yet certain. Be careful if a report doesn't say who gave the facts. Most importantly, check a news story before you share it.
watch.summary.source: This animated video is about how to choose your news. Not long ago, most people got news from a few newspapers and TV channels. Now the internet brings much more news, from many more people. Different sources may even disagree about the facts. The video gives some tips. When you can, find the first source, like the real report or speech. When a big story is still happening, do not check every few minutes. Wait for clear facts. Read the same story in more than one place. Look for words like “think”, “likely” or “probably”. They show that a report is not sure. Be careful when a report does not say who gave the facts. Most important, check a story before you share it.

read.sections.0.text.back: Messages spread very fast through phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some contain mistakes that were not on purpose, and some are completely made up. A message in capital letters that says "Spread this now" can feel urgent, but that does not make it true. To judge any claim, first find out its source. Post A has no name, date, or link, so no one can know where it really came from. Post B is a signed announcement on the learning centre's own page, and dated today. Post B also gives evidence: the exact hours and a clear reason why the learning centre is closed. A clear source with specific details is usually more trustworthy.
read.sections.0.text.source: Messages spread very fast on phones and messaging apps. Some are true, some are honest mistakes and some are completely invented. A message with capital letters that says “Share now” can feel urgent, but that does not make it true. To judge any claim, first identify its source. Post A has no name, no date and no link, so nobody can tell where it really came from. Post B is a signed notice on the centre's own page, and it is dated today. It also gives evidence: exact times and a clear reason for the closure. A clear source with specific details is usually more trustworthy.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Messages spread fast through phones. Some are true. Some are wrong. A post in big letters that says "Spread this now" can feel important. But that does not make it true. When you see a claim, ask about its source. Who made it? Post A has no name and no date. Post B comes from the learning centre itself. It has a date. There is also evidence, like the exact hours. So Post B is easier to trust.

read.sections.1.text.back: Even a real photo can mislead people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the photo is from last year, so the photo cannot tell us anything about tomorrow. The date, place, and reason a photo was taken are the photo's context, and context changes the meaning of a photo. Photos can also be edited with apps, or even made by a computer. The giant fish in Message F looks strange around its edges, and no one else has a picture of it. If a photo or story feels shocking, look for the same news from another trustworthy source.
read.sections.1.text.note: Review: English "a real locked door" stresses that the photo is genuine; "pintu yang benar-benar terkunci" says the door really is locked. Consider "pintu asli yang terkunci" to match the point that a real photo can still mislead. | Fixed after review: "a real locked door": the photo is real, not that the door is really locked.
read.sections.1.text.source: Even a real photo can mislead people. Post C shows a real locked door, but the photo is from last year, so it cannot tell us anything about tomorrow. The date, the place and the reason for a photo are its context, and context changes what a photo means. Photos can also be edited with apps, or even made by a computer. The giant fish in Message F looks strange at the edges, and nobody else has a picture of it. When a photo or story seems surprising, look for the same news from another trusted source.

No one else has a photo of it. Look for that news in another place you trust.

read.sections.2.text.back: A rumour is a story that spreads from person to person without evidence. Message D and Message E both look like rumours. Message D does not explain who is giving out the free boots. Message E says "doctors don't want you to know this", but does not name a single doctor or health organisation. Before sharing any message, try to check whether it is true. Ask three questions: Who made it? When was the message made? What is the evidence? Then compare with a trustworthy source, like a teacher, a health worker, or an official announcement. If you cannot check whether a message is true, it is usually safer not to forward it.
